items.title: Week 1: Orientation
items.body_brief: Module header for Week 1. Sets the tone that this course is about your real workplace problem, not a case study. Signal that the week closes with a committed problem choice and an initial stakeholder map.

items.title: Welcome and How This Course Works
items.body_brief: Short orientation page. Explain the 10-week arc (orientation, four two-week sprints, capstone), the expectation that every participant will pick a real problem from their own workplace and talk to real stakeholders, and the weekly time commitment. Be direct. Assume professional judgment. Acknowledge that time is tight and every activity is designed to deliver value the same week it is assigned.

items.title: Cohort Introductions
items.body_brief: Peer introductions. Ask each participant to post a short introduction: their role, their organization in broad strokes, and one workplace situation where AI has already shown up or is being pushed onto them. Ask them to respond to two others whose context differs from their own. Keep it professional and concrete, not a get-to-know-you exercise.

items.title: Orientation Check
items.body_brief: Short low-stakes quiz (4-6 questions) confirming participants understand the course expectations: problems are real and from their workplace, stakeholder conversations are required, AI is used as a partner rather than a replacement for thinking, and each sprint produces a visible artifact. Use short-answer and true/false questions. This is a check for understanding, not a gate.

items.title: Choose Your Problem
items.body_brief: The autonomy moment. Ask the participant to commit to the workplace problem they will work on for the next nine weeks. They should name the problem in one or two sentences, describe why it matters in their organization right now, who is affected, and what makes them think it is worth 10 weeks of attention. The problem must be real, current, and from their own workplace. Do not accept hypothetical or historical problems. Make clear they can refine the problem statement later, but the topic commitment stays.

rubric.description: Problem is real, current, and grounded in the participant's own workplace
Stakes and affected people are named concretely, not in abstractions
Written with professional specificity: named roles, real functions, actual consequences

items.title: Initial Stakeholder Map
items.body_brief: Ask the participant to produce a first-pass map of the stakeholders connected to their chosen problem. Upload a diagram, sketch, or annotated list (photo of whiteboard is fine). For each stakeholder, capture their role, how they are connected to the problem, and whether they have authority, influence, or just skin in the game. At least one of these people will be interviewed in Sprint 1, so ask the participant to flag who they plan to approach first and why.

rubric.description: Stakeholders are named by role and relationship to the problem, not generic labels
Authority, influence, and impact are distinguished
A clear first-conversation candidate is identified with a reason

items.title: Sprint 1: Surfacing the Problem
items.body_brief: Module header for Sprint 1 (Weeks 2-3). Theme: move from a vague concern to a first articulated problem statement, with one real stakeholder conversation behind it.

items.title: Sprint 1 Briefing
items.body_brief: Brief the sprint. Explain that this sprint produces three things: a first-pass written problem statement, a candid audit of the assumptions baked into it, and notes from one real conversation with a stakeholder. Emphasize that the goal is not a polished statement; the goal is surfacing what the participant actually believes about the problem so it can be tested. Keep the briefing short and operational.

items.title: First-Pass Problem Statement
items.body_brief: Ask the participant to write a first-pass problem statement in their own words, without using AI. Roughly one paragraph. It should name the problem, who is affected, why it matters now, and what a better state would look like. This draft will almost certainly be wrong in ways they cannot yet see. That is the point. They will return to this draft at the end of the course and compare.

rubric.description: Problem, affected people, stakes, and desired state are each present
Writing is concrete, grounded in the participant's real context
Draft was produced without AI (participant confirms)

items.title: Assumption Audit with AI
items.body_brief: Ask the participant to use an AI tool to surface the assumptions embedded in their first-pass problem statement. They should share the statement with the AI, ask it to list the assumptions it detects, and push back on the ones that feel wrong or too generic. Submit a short write-up covering: the assumptions AI surfaced, which ones genuinely surprised the participant, which ones they rejected and why, and one assumption they now want to test with a stakeholder. This is the first structured experience of the partnership: AI generates breadth, the participant exercises judgment.

rubric.description: Assumptions surfaced by AI are listed clearly
Participant's own judgment is visible: what they kept, what they rejected, why
At least one assumption is named as testable with a specific stakeholder

items.title: Listening Conversation with a Stakeholder
items.body_brief: The stakeholder touchpoint for Sprint 1. Ask the participant to hold one real conversation with a stakeholder from their map. The purpose is listening, not pitching: they want to hear how the stakeholder actually sees the problem. Upload notes from the conversation (photo of handwritten notes, typed doc, or transcript is fine) along with a one-paragraph debrief: what surprised them, what contradicted their first-pass statement, and what one follow-up question they now want to ask. No role-play. No simulated stakeholder. A real person from their organization.

rubric.description: Evidence of a real conversation with a named stakeholder (role, relationship)
Notes capture what the stakeholder said, not what the participant wanted to hear
Debrief names at least one surprise or contradiction with the first-pass statement

items.title: Sprint 1 Peer Exchange
items.body_brief: Peer discussion closing the sprint. Ask each participant to post one assumption their stakeholder conversation shifted, and one question they are now stuck on. Respond to two peers whose organizational context is different from their own. The purpose is cross-context exposure, not validation.

items.title: Sprint 2: Scope and Stakeholders
items.body_brief: Module header for Sprint 2 (Weeks 4-5). Theme: define what is in and out of the problem, and deepen stakeholder understanding through a structured interview with someone whose perspective differs from the Sprint 1 contact.

items.title: Sprint 2 Briefing
items.body_brief: Brief the sprint. The participant will draft an explicit scope (what counts as part of this problem, what does not), interview a stakeholder whose relationship to the problem is different from the Sprint 1 contact (an authority figure, an affected end user, or a cross-functional partner), and synthesize what the two stakeholder perspectives imply for the frame. Note that disagreement between stakeholders is expected and useful.

items.title: Scope and Boundaries Draft
items.body_brief: Ask the participant to draft an explicit scope for their problem. Structure: what is in scope (the parts of the problem this work will address), what is out of scope (adjacent issues this work will not address), and why those boundaries make sense given their role, authority, and timeline. AI may be used to brainstorm candidates for the in/out lists, but the reasoning for the boundaries must be the participant's own.

rubric.description: In-scope and out-of-scope items are specific, not generic
Boundary reasoning reflects the participant's actual role, authority, and constraints
Scope is tight enough to be tractable in 10 weeks

items.title: Second Stakeholder Interview
items.body_brief: The stakeholder touchpoint for Sprint 2. Ask the participant to interview a second stakeholder, chosen for a perspective that differs from the Sprint 1 contact. This is a structured interview: the participant prepares questions in advance (AI can help draft), runs the conversation, and uploads the interview plan plus notes or recording. Emphasize that the goal is to hear a view that might contradict the first one, not to confirm what they already believe.

rubric.description: Interview plan shows intentional question design tied to the problem frame
Stakeholder is genuinely different in role or perspective from the Sprint 1 contact
Notes capture what the stakeholder said, including anything that cuts against the participant's current view

items.title: Synthesize What You Heard
items.body_brief: Ask the participant to synthesize across the two stakeholder conversations. Where do the perspectives agree? Where do they conflict? What does each stakeholder see that the other does not? Which tensions are real and must be navigated in the problem frame, and which are just differences in language? AI may help organize themes, but the judgment about which tensions matter is the participant's.

rubric.description: Points of agreement and disagreement between stakeholders are named concretely
At least one real tension is identified and its implication for the frame explained
Participant's own judgment about what matters is visible, not just AI-generated themes

items.title: Sprint 2 Peer Exchange
items.body_brief: Peer discussion closing the sprint. Ask each participant to share one scope call they made that was harder than expected and one stakeholder tension they are still working through. Respond to two peers, ideally naming a tension in their frame that they may not be seeing.

items.title: Sprint 3: AI Fit and Success Criteria
items.module: Sprint 3: AI Fit and Success Criteria
items.body_brief: Module header for Sprint 3 (Weeks 6-7). Theme: test whether AI genuinely belongs in the solution space for this problem, define what success would look like, and validate the success criteria with a stakeholder.

items.title: Sprint 3 Briefing
items.module: Sprint 3: AI Fit and Success Criteria
items.body_brief: Brief the sprint. The participant will examine whether AI actually adds value to this problem or is being forced in (AI fit analysis), draft concrete success criteria, test those criteria with a stakeholder, and produce a clean map of what AI contributes vs. what the participant must contribute. Be direct: if AI does not belong in the solution, the frame should say so.

items.title: AI-Fit Analysis
items.module: Sprint 3: AI Fit and Success Criteria
items.body_brief: Ask the participant to analyze whether AI genuinely fits this problem. Questions to address: what specifically would AI do in a solution? What signals that AI belongs here (scale, breadth, pattern recognition across more data than a person can hold)? What signals that AI does not (relationship work, one-off judgment calls, high-consequence decisions where accountability must stay human)? If AI does not fit, say so. A participant who concludes their problem is not actually an AI problem has done the work correctly.

rubric.description: Specific AI roles in the solution are named, not generic 'use AI' claims
Signals for and against AI fit are balanced; participant takes a defensible position
Conclusion is grounded in the participant's organizational context, not generic AI hype

items.title: Success Criteria with a Stakeholder
items.module: Sprint 3: AI Fit and Success Criteria
items.body_brief: The stakeholder touchpoint for Sprint 3. Ask the participant to draft success criteria for their problem (what would have to be true for them to call this work a success?) and then hold a short conversation with a stakeholder to test those criteria. Ideally the stakeholder is someone with authority over whether this work would be considered successful. Upload the draft criteria, notes from the conversation, and a revised set of criteria reflecting what they heard.

rubric.description: Draft criteria are specific and measurable or observable, not aspirational
Real stakeholder conversation is documented, with the stakeholder's role clear
Revised criteria reflect what the stakeholder said, not just what the participant thought

items.title: Human and AI Contribution Map
items.module: Sprint 3: AI Fit and Success Criteria
items.body_brief: Ask the participant to produce a clear two-column map for their problem: what AI would contribute (scale, breadth, speed on specific tasks) and what the participant and their stakeholders must contribute (judgment, relationships, organizational knowledge, accountability for decisions and their consequences). For each entry, name the specific thing, not a category. The participant should be able to point to a moment in their work so far where they contributed something AI could not have provided, and use it as evidence.

rubric.description: Contributions are specific and tied to this problem, not generic statements about AI
Human contributions include judgment, relationships, and accountability (not just domain knowledge)
At least one concrete moment from the participant's own work is cited as evidence

items.title: Sprint 3 Peer Critique
items.module: Sprint 3: AI Fit and Success Criteria
items.body_brief: Peer discussion closing the sprint. Ask each participant to post their AI-fit conclusion in one sentence and their sharpest success criterion. Respond to two peers by pushing back: is the AI-fit conclusion actually supported by what they described, or is it just 'AI seems useful'? Is the success criterion specific enough that a stakeholder would know when it was met? Direct peer critique, not affirmation.

items.title: Sprint 4: Validated Framing
items.body_brief: Module header for Sprint 4 (Weeks 8-9). Theme: integrate everything from Sprints 1-3 into a complete problem frame, validate it with a decision-maker, and revise based on what they heard.

items.title: Sprint 4 Briefing
items.body_brief: Brief the sprint. This sprint produces the integrated problem frame that will be demonstrated in the capstone. The participant pulls together the problem statement, scope, stakeholder perspectives, success criteria, and human/AI contribution split into one coherent document. Then they validate it with a decision-maker (someone with authority over whether this problem gets worked on) and revise. The frame should be tight enough that a stranger to the organization could understand what problem is being framed, why, and for whom.

items.title: Integrated Problem Frame
items.body_brief: Ask the participant to write the integrated problem frame: problem statement, stakeholders and their perspectives, scope, success criteria, and the human/AI contribution split. Roughly two to three pages. This replaces the Sprint 1 first-pass statement. AI is a legitimate drafting partner for this document, but every section must reflect decisions the participant has made and can defend.

rubric.description: All five elements are present and internally consistent
Document is written for a reader who does not know the organization
Participant's professional judgment is visible in the framing choices, not just AI phrasing

items.title: Validation Conversation with a Decision-Maker
items.body_brief: The stakeholder touchpoint for Sprint 4. Ask the participant to share the integrated frame with someone in their organization who has authority over whether this problem gets worked on (a manager, a director, a client lead). The goal is validation and pushback, not approval. Upload the frame as shared, notes from the conversation, and the specific pieces of feedback that will change the frame.

rubric.description: The decision-maker is genuinely senior or authoritative for this problem
Conversation notes include pushback, not just agreement
Specific feedback-driven changes to the frame are identified

items.title: Revise Based on What You Learned
items.body_brief: Ask the participant to revise the integrated problem frame based on the validation conversation. Submit the revised frame along with a short change log: what changed, what stayed, and why. If nothing changed, that is a finding worth defending in writing. This revised frame is what the participant will demonstrate in the capstone.

rubric.description: Revisions are traceable to specific feedback, not cosmetic edits
Change log explains the reasoning behind each substantive change or non-change
Revised frame is tighter and more defensible than the draft

items.title: Sprint 4 Peer Exchange
items.body_brief: Peer discussion closing the sprint. Ask each participant to share the single most important thing their decision-maker said, and how their frame changed (or did not) because of it. Respond to two peers. This is the last peer exchange before the capstone, so signal that the cohort will see these frames again in Week 10.

items.title: Week 10: Capstone
items.body_brief: Module header for Week 10. The capstone: demonstrate the validated problem frame to peers and stakeholders and articulate the human judgment behind it.

items.title: Capstone Brief
items.body_brief: Brief the capstone. Explain what participants will produce: a short demonstration of their validated problem frame (a written walk-through, a recorded presentation, or a slide deck with narration - participant chooses the format) shared with both peers and at least one stakeholder from their map, plus a written articulation of the human judgment they brought to the work. Make clear this is a competence moment, not a test: they will be showing what they can now do that they could not do in Week 1.

items.title: Capstone Demonstration
items.body_brief: Ask the participant to demonstrate their validated problem frame. Format is their choice: a recorded walk-through (video or audio), a narrated slide deck, or a polished written artifact. The demonstration should cover the problem, stakeholders, scope, success criteria, human/AI contributions, and how the frame evolved across the sprints. Ask them to share the demonstration with at least one stakeholder from their map and include that stakeholder's response (written, recorded, or summarized) as part of the upload.

rubric.description: Demonstration clearly conveys the full validated frame to an outside audience
Evolution of the frame across sprints is visible (first-pass vs. final)
At least one stakeholder's response to the final frame is included
Format choice suits the participant's context and is professionally executed

items.title: Human Judgment Articulation
items.body_brief: Ask the participant to write a short, direct articulation of the human judgment they brought to this work - the things AI could not have provided. Specific prompts: what organizational context shaped the frame that AI did not know? Which stakeholder relationships influenced the scope? Which prioritization calls were judgment calls that could have gone another way? Where in the process did they slow down and override what AI suggested, and why? One to two pages. This is the articulation that Outcome 4 asks for, and it is the artifact that differentiates a completer from someone who used AI to write a problem statement.

rubric.description: Organizational context the participant contributed is named concretely
Stakeholder-relationship and prioritization judgments are made visible
At least one moment of overriding or redirecting AI is described with reasoning

items.title: Closing Cohort Reflection
items.body_brief: Closing discussion. Ask each participant to post: one thing they can now do with a workplace problem that they could not do in Week 1, and one thing they want to carry forward into Course 2. Respond to two peers whose growth or direction surprised them. The intent is relatedness and a visible close to the cohort arc, not summative reflection.
